cues.text: Welcome to Coordination Compounds.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Our first habit is to read the brackets before counting anything.
A coordination entity contains a central atom or ion and its directly bonded
ligands.
A ligand donates an electron pair through a donor atom.
Species outside the brackets are counterions, not automatically ligands.
Consider the cobalt complex on the board.
Three chloride counterions require the bracketed entity to have charge
positive
three.
The abbreviation e n stands for ethane one two diamine.
Each of these ligands is neutral, so cobalt has oxidation state plus three.
Now count donor atoms separately.
Each e n attaches through two nitrogen atoms.
Three such bidentate ligands give six directly attached donors.
The coordination number is six, not three.
Oxidation state, complex charge, ligand count and donor count are four
different quantities.
Werner's primary valency is associated with oxidation state, while secondary
valency is associated with coordination number and directed bonding.
Water and ammonia are normally monodentate.
A chelating ligand attaches through several donor atoms and forms a ring with
the metal.
E D T A can bind through six donor atoms in a common hexadentate arrangement.
An ambidentate ligand is different: it can use alternative donor atoms.
Nitrite can bind through nitrogen or oxygen, but that does not mean it
normally
binds through both simultaneously.
For a second charge check, take hexacyanidoferrate with overall charge
negative
four.
Six cyanide ligands contribute negative six.
The iron oxidation state must be plus two to give negative four overall.
Write that short charge equation before assigning any electronic
configuration.
The ligand's charge belongs in the charge balance; its denticity belongs in
the
donor count.
Naming becomes easier after charge balance.
Name ligands alphabetically, ignoring multiplicative prefixes, then name the
metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals.
Ammonia is called ammine, with two m letters, and water is aqua.
An anionic complex uses a metal name ending in ate; iron uses ferrate.
Thus the potassium salt of the negative four hexacyanidoferrate ion is
potassium hexacyanidoferrate, two.
The Roman numeral refers to iron's oxidation state, not the ion's charge.
Now consider the cobalt salt with four ammonia ligands, two chlorido ligands
inside the brackets and one chloride outside.
The complex has charge positive one.
Four neutral ammonia ligands contribute zero and the two bound chlorides
contribute negative two.
Cobalt is therefore plus three.
Ammine precedes chlorido alphabetically.
The name is tetraammine dichlorido cobalt, three, chloride, as written
together
on the board.
Its octahedral geometry allows cis and trans forms; the formula alone does not
tell us which one we have.
Next, distinguish bound chloride from ionizable chloride.
Our worked salt has five ammonia ligands and one chloride inside the brackets,
with two chlorides outside.
We assume an immediate silver nitrate test that leaves the coordination sphere
intact.
Under that assumption only the two outer chlorides form silver chloride.
A sample containing zero point zero one zero zero mole of salt therefore gives
zero point zero two zero zero mole of silver chloride.
Multiply by one hundred forty three point five grams per mole to obtain two
point eight seven grams.
Cobalt is still plus three and its coordination number is six.
Counting all three chlorines as precipitated chloride would ignore the test's
stated assumption.
Bound ligands are not permanently impossible to displace; reaction conditions
and time matter.
In this question, the intact sphere assumption tells us exactly what to count.
Coordination number is useful, but it does not uniquely fix geometry.
Six donors commonly give an octahedral environment.
Four can give tetrahedral or square planar geometry.
In elementary valence bond language these are described using orbital
combinations such as s p three for tetrahedral and d s p two for square
planar.
These labels are a model, not a complete explanation of spectra.
Isomerism needs a separate check.
Structural isomers differ in connectivity or in which species lie inside the
coordination sphere.
Linkage isomers use different donor atoms of an ambidentate ligand.
Ionization isomers exchange a coordinated ion with a counterion.
A drawing merely rotated on the page is not a new isomer.
For square planar platinum with two ammonia and two chloride ligands, adjacent
chlorides define the cis form, while opposite chlorides define trans.
The angle between the two platinum to chloride bond directions is ninety
degrees in cis and one hundred eighty in trans.
These are spatial arrangements with the same connectivity.
An octahedral complex with three monodentate A ligands and three monodentate B
ligands can have facial and meridional forms.
In the facial form, the three A donors occupy a triangular face.
Every A to metal to A angle is ninety degrees.
In the meridional form, one pair of A ligands is opposite, giving a one
hundred
eighty degree angle.
Draw or label the six positions before counting arrangements.
Optical isomers are non superimposable mirror images.
The cobalt complex with three bidentate e n ligands can form such a pair.
Equal amounts of both mirror forms make a racemic mixture with no net optical
rotation.
That does not make the individual structures identical.
Detailed three dimensional optical drawings remain further practice.
First establish connectivity and geometry, then ask which particular kind of
isomerism is possible.
Crystal field theory separates the five d orbitals into groups with different
energies.
In an octahedral field, the three t two g orbitals are lower and the two e g
orbitals are higher.
Relative to the barycentre, a t two g electron contributes minus zero point
four delta octahedral, and an e g electron contributes plus zero point six
delta octahedral.
Those contributions alone exclude pairing energy.
Consider a d six metal ion.
If splitting is small compared with the cost of pairing, the high spin
arrangement has four electrons in t two g and two in e g.
Its orbital occupancy contains four unpaired electrons and one pair.
If splitting is sufficiently large, the low spin arrangement puts all six
electrons into the lower set as three pairs.
There are then no unpaired electrons.
Let's calculate the high spin field contribution.
Four times minus zero point four, plus two times zero point six, gives minus
zero point four delta octahedral.
The low spin field contribution is six times minus zero point four, or minus
two point four delta octahedral.
Now include P as the cost per electron pair.
High spin has energy minus zero point four delta plus P.
Low spin has minus two point four delta plus three P.
Comparing only the negative field terms would miss the extra pairing cost.
With delta equal to two hundred fifty kilojoules per mole and P equal to one
hundred eighty, high spin gives positive eighty and low spin negative sixty
kilojoules per mole on the same chosen energy reference.
Low spin minus high spin is negative one hundred forty.
Low spin is lower by one hundred forty kilojoules per mole in this simplified
model.
The crossover is when the octahedral splitting equals the pairing energy.
Do not transfer this octahedral orbital diagram unchanged to a square planar
or
tetrahedral complex.
Unpaired electrons produce paramagnetism.
An all paired arrangement is diamagnetic.
The spin only magnetic moment is the square root of n times n plus two, in
Bohr
magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
This is an approximation; orbital contributions can matter.
Our high spin octahedral d six example has four unpaired electrons.
The square root of four times six is about four point nine zero Bohr
magnetons.
Low spin d six has no unpaired electrons.
Now compare the two nickel complexes on the board.
Each has four singly negative ligands and total charge negative two, so both
contain nickel in oxidation state plus two.
Nickel two has a d eight configuration, after removal of the two four s
electrons from neutral nickel.
The chloride complex is usually tetrahedral with two unpaired electrons.
Its spin only moment is the square root of eight, about two point eight three
Bohr magnetons.
The cyanide complex is square planar and all paired, so it is diamagnetic.
The same metal, oxidation state and coordination number did not guarantee the
same geometry or magnetism.
Colour needs another check.
Absorption between split d levels can remove visible wavelengths, leaving a
complementary transmitted or reflected colour.
Ligands, oxidation state and geometry affect the splitting.
Charge transfer transitions can also produce colour, so d zero or d ten does
not guarantee that every compound is colourless.
Complex formation is useful in qualitative analysis, including the deep blue
copper ammine species in aqueous ammonia, and in biological metal binding,
such
as iron in haem proteins and magnesium in chlorophyll.
Finish with the sequence: complex charge, oxidation state, donor count, d
electron count, geometry, then properties.
Use the twelve original practice questions and the seven worked examples in
the
written companion.
This is a recorded Unit twelve foundation, not exhaustive coverage or official
past paper material.
Isomerism can change which ion is outside the coordination sphere or which
atom
binds to the metal.
Compare a cobalt complex with five neutral ammonia ligands and coordinated
bromide, accompanied by a sulfate counterion, with one containing coordinated
sulfate and an external bromide.
Cobalt is plus three in each.
In the first case, the complex charge is plus two; in the second, it is plus
one.
The overall elemental inventory is unchanged, but the counterions differ.
This illustrates ionization isomerism, assuming the stated coordination
spheres
persist under the test conditions.
Linkage isomerism is different.
An ambidentate nitrite ligand can attach through nitrogen or through oxygen,
giving different metal to donor connectivity without exchanging the external
counterion.
Ambidentate does not mean both donor atoms necessarily bind simultaneously to
this metal.
A bidentate ligand instead supplies two donor attachments in the specified
complex.
Classify the structural change before applying an isomer name.
Formula brackets identify the coordination sphere, so moving a group across a
bracket changes chemical information rather than merely changing typography.
For an octahedral complex with three identical A ligands and three identical B
ligands, facial and meridional arrangements are distinct geometrical isomers.
Imagine six ligand positions on the positive and negative x, y and z axes.
Opposite ends of the same axis are trans, while positions on different axes
are cis.
A facial arrangement places the three A ligands at positive x, positive y and
positive z.
Every A pair is cis, and the three positions form one face of the octahedron.
A meridional arrangement can place A at positive x, negative x and positive z.
The first two form a trans pair, while the other two A pairs are cis.
The schematic shows these position labels so the classification does not
depend
on an ambiguous flat sketch.
Rotating an entire complex does not create a new isomer.
Exchanging ligand positions can.
These fac and mer labels apply to this octahedral three plus three pattern; do
not reuse them for every six coordinate formula without checking its ligand
arrangement.
A chelating ligand binds through multiple donor atoms to the same central
metal
and closes a ring.
Ethane one two diamine, commonly abbreviated e n, can bind through its two
nitrogen atoms.
Three such ligands around cobalt give six donor attachments, so the
coordination number is six although there are only three ligand molecules.
With neutral diamine ligands and complex charge plus three, cobalt has
oxidation state plus three.
An octahedral tris chelate arrangement can have two nonsuperimposable mirror
image forms, conventionally described by delta and lambda helicity labels.
They have the same connectivity but a different three dimensional handed
arrangement.
Mirror images that can be superimposed do not constitute an optical isomer
pair.
A flat donor count table alone cannot establish handedness; a spatial model is
needed for that assignment.
Individual enantiomers can rotate plane polarized light, while an equal
mixture
has cancelling rotations under the same conditions.
Delta and lambda specify structural helicity; they do not automatically
predict
the sign of measured optical rotation.
Keep ligand count, donor count, oxidation state and chirality as separate
questions.
Complex stability is an equilibrium question that needs a defined reaction.
Suppose a metal M binds one ligand L to make M L, then binds another to make M
L two.
Define the first and second stepwise formation constants from those two
equilibria.
Adding the reactions gives metal plus two ligands forming the bis ligand
complex.
Multiplying the stepwise constants gives the overall formation constant beta
two.
With illustrative dimensionless constants ten to the four and ten to the
three,
beta two is ten to the seven.
It is not their sum, and the second constant need not always exceed the first.
Thermodynamic constants use activities; concentration ratios are
approximations
under specified solution conditions.
A large overall formation constant favours the complex relative to free metal
and free ligand for that defined equilibrium, but the actual composition also
depends on ligand availability, competing reactions and mass balances.
Thermodynamic stability is distinct from kinetic inertness.
A complex can be strongly favoured at equilibrium while exchanging ligands
rapidly, or react slowly even when a different product is favoured.
Coordination compounds connect reaction chemistry with biological and
analytical functions.
Chlorophyll contains magnesium in its coordinated pigment framework, while
haem
groups contain iron in a porphyrin environment.
Vitamin B twelve contains cobalt.
These metal identities are useful starting facts, but they do not imply that
every metal ion has the same biological function in every ligand environment.
In qualitative analysis, complex formation can change the concentration of a
free metal ion and thereby affect precipitation or dissolution equilibria.
Such reasoning requires the competing equilibrium constants and solution
conditions.
In a standard silver complex example, two cyanide ligands each have charge
minus one.
A complex charge of minus one therefore places silver at oxidation state plus
one.
Its formation does not itself require a change in the silver oxidation state.
Complex formation is also used in extraction and purification chemistry
because
ligands can stabilize selected dissolved metal species.
Keep ligand binding, redox conversion and precipitation conceptually separate,
then connect them through balanced equations when a problem supplies enough
data.
The purpose here is interpreting chemical roles and charge balance, rather
than
prescribing an experimental procedure.
Coordination isomerism concerns how ligands are distributed between a complex
cation and a complex anion.
Compare a salt containing hexaamminecobalt three plus and hexacyanidochromate
three minus with a salt containing hexaamminechromium three plus and
hexacyanidocobaltate three minus.
The total atom inventory is the same, but the metal to ligand connections
differ.
In each cation, six neutral ammonia ligands surround a metal in oxidation
state
plus three.
In each anion, six cyanido ligands of charge minus one surround a metal in
oxidation state plus three, giving overall charge minus three.
Six donor atoms coordinate to each metal in this monodentate example.
This exchange is different from linkage isomerism, where one ambidentate
ligand
changes
its
donor atom, and different from ionization isomerism, where coordinated and
counter ions exchange roles.
A formula comparison should establish the same overall composition before
applying an isomer label.
Merely changing an oxidation number in a written name does not create a valid
pair.
The example classifies connectivity; it does not imply that every conceivable
exchanged salt has equal stability or can be prepared under identical
conditions.
Water shown in a coordination formula can be a ligand or a molecule of
crystallization.
Compare hexaaquachromium three chloride, with six water ligands inside the
coordination sphere and three chloride counter ions, against
pentaaquachloridochromium three chloride monohydrate.
In the second compound, five waters and one chloride occupy six donor
positions
around chromium.
Two chlorides remain outside and one water is outside as water of
crystallization.
Both have the same total inventory of chromium, three chlorines and six
waters,
while their coordination spheres differ.
This is a hydrate or solvate isomerism comparison.
In an ideal immediate chloride precipitation test that leaves the coordination
sphere intact, one mole of the first compound gives three moles of silver
chloride, while one mole of the second gives two.
For zero point zero one zero zero mole of each, with supplied silver chloride
molar mass one hundred forty three point five grams per mole, the predicted
masses are four point three zero five and two point eight seven zero grams.
Slow ligand substitution or other side processes can invalidate a simple outer
sphere count, so the test conditions and time scale matter.
Crystal field stabilization is measured relative to a chosen orbital energy
barycentre.
For an octahedral d three ion in the elementary model, three electrons occupy
the lower three orbitals singly.
Each contributes minus zero point four times the octahedral splitting, giving
total minus one point two times that splitting, with three unpaired electrons.
A tetrahedral d three ion instead fills two lower orbitals singly, then places
the third electron in one of the upper three orbitals under the usual high
spin
assumption.
Lower orbitals contribute minus zero point six times the tetrahedral splitting
each; the upper electron contributes plus zero point four, giving net minus
zero point eight times the tetrahedral splitting.
Both arrangements have three unpaired electrons, so equal unpaired counts do
not imply equal orbital stabilization or equal geometry.
In a supplied ideal comparison, the tetrahedral splitting is four ninths of
the
octahedral value for otherwise comparable fields.
If octahedral splitting is eighteen thousand reciprocal centimetres,
tetrahedral splitting is eight thousand, and the two stabilizations are minus
twenty one thousand six hundred and minus six thousand four hundred reciprocal
centimetres.
Actual geometry selection involves more than this one energy contribution.
Ligand count and coordination number are different quantities.
In a simple metal complex with one fully bound hexadentate EDTA ligand, the
ligand uses two nitrogen and four oxygen donor atoms.
One ligand can therefore account for six donor positions.
Treating six donor atoms as six separate EDTA molecules would give the wrong
composition and titration ratio.
Consider a supplied one to one metal binding model at a suitable buffered p H,
with no interfering ions.
A twenty five point zero millilitre metal aliquot consumes twenty point zero
millilitres of zero point zero one zero zero molar EDTA.
Titrant amount is zero point zero zero zero two zero zero mole, equal to metal
amount in the stated model.
Dividing by zero point zero two five zero litre gives metal concentration zero
point zero zero eight zero zero molar.
EDTA protonation and metal hydrolysis depend on p H, so its effective binding
strength is conditional; a large formal formation constant alone does not
guarantee quantitative titration in every solution.
The calculation assumes suitable reaction completion and endpoint detection.
It illustrates ligand denticity and analytical stoichiometry, not an
instruction to conduct a titration without a laboratory protocol.
A crystal field contribution alone is not the total cost of changing spin
state.
For an octahedral d five ion in the elementary model, high spin places three
electrons in the lower set and two in the upper set, all unpaired.
Its crystal field contribution is zero, and it has no electron pairs.
Low spin places all five electrons in the lower set, giving two pairs and one
unpaired electron.
Its crystal field contribution is minus two times the octahedral splitting.
If each additional pair costs P, the low spin energy relative to high spin is
minus two delta plus two P.
With supplied splitting eighteen thousand reciprocal centimetres and pairing
cost twenty thousand in the same units, the difference is plus four thousand.
High spin is favoured by this limited comparison.
The low spin field term is negative, yet its extra pairing cost is larger.
Spin only moments are approximately five point nine two and one point seven
three Bohr magnetons respectively.
Real spin energetics require more detailed interactions than this simplified
accounting.
An absorption wavelength can estimate a level separation when the transition
assignment is supplied.
In a simplified octahedral d one example, suppose the band maximum at six
hundred nanometres represents the lower to upper d level splitting.
Use the supplied molar constant N A h c equal to zero point one one nine six
two six joule metre per mole.
Dividing by six hundred times ten to the minus nine metre gives about one
hundred ninety nine point four kilojoules per mole.
A second assigned band at five hundred nanometres corresponds to about two
hundred thirty nine point three kilojoules per mole, a larger splitting.
Shorter wavelength means higher photon energy.
Do not confuse energy per photon with energy per mole of absorbed photons.
Nor does an absorption maximum directly name the observed solution colour: the
transmitted or reflected spectrum depends on which wavelengths are removed and
on the full band shape.
Other complexes may have multiple d transitions or charge transfer bands, so
the assignment of a measured maximum to one splitting must be justified rather
than assumed universally.
A larger formation constant does not alone fix which complex dominates when
free ligand concentrations differ.
Consider a supplied dilute solution model with one metal ion and two competing
neutral monodentate ligands, L and X.
The complexes are M L two and M X two, with overall formation constants one
hundred million and one million respectively, using consistent concentration
conventions.
Free ligand concentrations are zero point zero zero one zero zero molar L and
zero point zero one zero zero molar X.
Dividing the two formation expressions cancels the same free metal
concentration.
The complex ratio is one hundred times the square of one tenth, which equals
one.
Thus the two complex concentrations are equal under these specified free
ligand
conditions.
The larger L formation constant is exactly offset by its lower free
concentration in this example.
Total ligand added is not automatically equal to free ligand concentration,
because binding and other equilibria can consume it.
The model omits mixed ligand complexes, protonation, hydrolysis and
precipitation.
Full speciation requires those extra balances when they are relevant.
Chelation often benefits from entropy, but its thermodynamic preference must
be
evaluated for a specified balanced reaction.
Consider an illustrative ligand exchange with supplied standard reaction
enthalpy plus six point zero zero kilojoules per mole and standard reaction
entropy plus forty point zero joules per mole kelvin.
At three hundred kelvin, the entropy term is twelve point zero kilojoules per
mole.
Standard reaction Gibbs energy is therefore minus six point zero zero
kilojoules per mole, despite the positive enthalpy.
With R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin, the
dimensionless equilibrium constant is exponential six thousand divided by
eight
point three one four times three hundred, about eleven point one.
This example shows how the entropy term can outweigh an enthalpy cost.
It does not claim that every chelate exchange has these signs or that counting
liberated molecules alone supplies a numerical entropy.
Solvation, ligand structure and standard states also matter.
Keep reaction stoichiometry and the stated temperature attached to each
thermodynamic quantity before making a stability comparison.
